proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(I_{ik}=\mathbf 1\{Z_{0i}=Z_{1k}\}\) and
\[
 W=\sum_{i=1}^{n_0}\sum_{k=1}^{n_1}I_{ik}.
\]
The labels are independent within each arm by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}uniform\mbox{-}cells}\), and the two arms are independent by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}arm\mbox{-}independence}\).  Consequently
\[
 \mathbb E I_{ik}=K^{-1}.
\]
Give \((i,k)\) the dependency neighborhood consisting of all \((i',k')\) with \(i'=i\) or \(k'=k\).  If \((i',k')\ne(i,k)\) belongs to this neighborhood, then exactly three independent uniform labels must agree, and hence
\[
 \mathbb E(I_{ik}I_{i'k'})=K^{-2}.
\]
Thus the quantities in Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}agg\mbox{-}poisson\mbox{-}approximation}\) are
\[
 b_1=\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1-1)}{K^2},
 \qquad
 b_2=\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1-2)}{K^2}.
\]
Because \(\mathbb EW=n_0n_1/K=\lambda_K\), that lemma and the definition of \(\varepsilon_K\) give
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathcal L(W),\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\right)
 \le 2(b_1+b_2)
 \le \frac{4n_0n_1(n_0+n_1)}{K^2}
 =4\varepsilon_K. \tag{1}
\]

Let \(B\) be the label-measurable event that a cell hit by both arms contains at least three observations in total.  If \(B\) occurs, then either two specified observations from arm zero and one specified observation from arm one have a common label, or the analogous event with the arms interchanged occurs.  Each such event has probability \(K^{-2}\).  The union bound therefore yields
\[
 \Pr(B)
 \le \frac{\binom{n_0}{2}n_1+n_0\binom{n_1}{2}}{K^2}
 =\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1-2)}{2K^2}
 \le\frac{\varepsilon_K}{2}. \tag{2}
\]
On \(B^{\mathrm c}\), each cross-arm matching pair is the unique pair in a cell containing exactly one observation from each arm, and conversely.  Hence \(M_K=W\) on \(B^{\mathrm c}\), so (1)--(2) imply
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathcal L(M_K),\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\right)
 \le 4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B). \tag{3}
\]
The laws of \(M_K\) and \(B\) depend only on the known sampling design, not on any sign array or on \(q\).

We next identify the parameter-bearing part of the unconditioned product mixture.  Denote by \(Q_{K,q}\) the observation law obtained by mixing the finite-array experiment with \(\Gamma_{K,q}\), before conditioning on \(A_{K,q}\).  For a cell containing exactly one observation from each arm, Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}conditional\mbox{-}bernoulli}\) gives, for \(x,y\in\{-1,1\}\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pr_q(X_0=x,X_1=y)
 &=\frac14\mathbb E_{\Gamma_{K,q}}
   \bigl[(1+2ax\theta_0)(1+2by\theta_1)\bigr]\\
 &=\frac{1+4abqxy}{4}
 =\frac{1+cqxy}{4}. \tag{4}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here the first equality uses conditional independence of the outcomes, while the second uses
\(\mathbb E\theta_0=\mathbb E\theta_1=0\),
\(\mathbb E(\theta_0\theta_1)=q\), and \(c=4ab\), all from the construction of \(\Gamma_{K,q}\).  It follows from (4) that the mark \(S=X_0X_1\) satisfies
\[
 \Pr_q(S=s)=\frac{1+cqs}{2},\qquad s\in\{-1,1\}, \tag{5}
\]
and, conditional on \(S\), the orientation \(X_0\) is fair and independent of \(q\).  Product mixing across cells makes the marks in distinct one-one cells independent.  Conditional on the occupancy pattern, every cell occupied by only one arm also has a \(q\)-free distribution: its latent sign has the fair marginal distribution under \(\Gamma_{K,q}\), even when that cell contains repeated observations from the same arm.  The occupancy pattern itself is parameter free.

Define \(\mathsf K_K^{\to}\) to retain from the full observation only the numbers of positive and negative marks among the \(M_K\) one-one cells.  This is a deterministic Markov kernel independent of \(q\).  Equations (4)--(5) show that under \(Q_{K,q}\), conditional on the parameter-free count \(M_K\), these marks are independent with probabilities \((1+cq)/2\) and \((1-cq)/2\).  Applying the same independent-marking kernel to a \(\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\) count gives exactly \(P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\).  Total variation contracts under Markov kernels, so (3) gives
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(Q_{K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\to},
 P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\right)
 \le 4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B). \tag{6}
\]
By Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}supported\mbox{-}mixture\mbox{-}legality}\),
\(\Gamma_{K,q}(A_{K,q}^{\mathrm c})\le\eta_K\).  Conditioning a probability law on an event of probability \(1-v\) changes it in total variation by \(v\); this follows directly by writing the conditional density as \(\mathbf 1_A/\Pr(A)\).  A further application of contraction therefore gives
\[
 \sup_{q\in\mathcal R_K^{\circ}(r)}
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\to},
 P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\right)
 \le4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B)+\eta_K
 \le5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K. \tag{7}
\]

For completeness, we construct a single reverse kernel.  The law of \(M_K\) is known and parameter free.  Couple an input \(N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\) maximally to a variable with this law: on the diagonal \((m,m)\), place mass equal to the minimum of the two count probabilities and distribute the residual masses by a fixed rule.  Conditional on the resulting value \(M_K=m\), sample a label-occupancy configuration from its known conditional law.  If \(N=M_K\) and \(B^{\mathrm c}\), randomly order the input's \(N_+\) positive and \(N_-\) negative marks among the one-one cells, draw their fair orientations, and draw all one-arm outcome blocks from their fair-sign mixture.  Equations (4)--(5) show that this conditional simulation equals the conditional law under \(Q_{K,q}\) and uses no \(q\).  If \(N\ne M_K\) or \(B\) occurs, use any fixed completion of the outcomes.  This defines a Markov kernel \(\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow}\) depending only on \(K,n_0,n_1,a,b,r\).

Under a coupling of the output of this kernel with \(Q_{K,q}\), disagreement can occur only when the coupled counts disagree or the target occupancy lies in \(B\).  Hence, using (2)--(3),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}
       \mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow},Q_{K,q}\right)
 &\le d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(
      \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K),\mathcal L(M_K)\right)+\Pr(B)\\
 &\le4\varepsilon_K+2\Pr(B)
 \le5\varepsilon_K. \tag{8}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The shell-conditioning bound adds at most \(\eta_K\), uniformly in \(q\), and proves the reverse inequality in the theorem.  Since total variation is at most one, (7)--(8) give the stated bound \(e_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K\}\).  The index of both decision experiments is the same fixed lattice value \(q\), and the loss target attached to that index is \(a-bq\); no realized random endpoint is substituted for this decision target.

It remains to prove the deterministic-array assertion.  Fix an array in \(\mathcal T_K(r)\), and put \(t_j=\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}\).  Enumerate the one-one cells using an independent, parameter-free uniform ordering; this does not alter the observed positive and negative mark counts.  By permutation symmetry of the uniform labels, conditional on \(M_K=m\), the ordered one-one cell labels are a uniform ordered sample without replacement from \(\{1,\ldots,K\}\).  Given label \(j\), Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}conditional\mbox{-}bernoulli}\) yields
\[
 \mathbb E_\theta(S\mid j)
 =\mathbb E_\theta(X_0\mid j)\mathbb E_\theta(X_1\mid j)
 =(2a\theta_{0j})(2b\theta_{1j})
 =ct_j. \tag{9}
\]
Because a \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued variable is determined by its mean, its conditional mass is \((1+ct_js)/2\).

Couple the ordered sample without replacement to \(m\) independent uniform cell labels.  The two samples can be made equal whenever the independent labels are distinct, since their conditional law on that event is uniform without replacement.  The union bound gives mismatch probability at most
\[
 \Pr\{\text{an independent label repeats}\}
 \le\frac{m(m-1)}{2K}. \tag{10}
\]
With independent uniform labels, (9), the identity
\(K^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^K t_j=\rho_K\), and independent outcome draws produce independent marks with mean \(c\rho_K\), exactly as in \(\mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho_K}\) conditional on its count.

Pointwise \(M_K\le W\).  Moreover, any two distinct indicators \(I_{ik}\) and \(I_{i'k'}\) have joint expectation \(K^{-2}\), whether or not they share one observation.  Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E\{M_K(M_K-1)\}
 \le\mathbb E\{W(W-1)\}
 =\frac{n_0n_1(n_0n_1-1)}{K^2}
 \le\lambda_K^2. \tag{11}
\]
Averaging (10) over \(M_K\), then applying (3) to replace its count law by \(\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\), gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(
   \mathcal L_\theta(M_K,S_1,\ldots,S_{M_K}),
   \mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho_K}\right)\\
 &\qquad\le4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B)
       +\frac{\mathbb E\{M_K(M_K-1)\}}{2K}\\
 &\qquad\le5\varepsilon_K+\frac{\lambda_K^2}{2K}. \tag{12}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Every upper bound in (12) is independent of the deterministic signs.  Capping it at one proves the asserted uniform bound \(e_K^{\mathrm{det}}\).

Write
\[
 e_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K\},\qquad
 \delta_K=2s_K+2/K,
\]
and set
\[
 u_K=e_K+\min\{1,\lambda_Kc\delta_K/2\},
 \qquad
 d_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\lambda_K^2/(2K)\}. \tag{13}
\]
We first compare the two honest-length frontiers at the finite intensity \(\lambda_K\).

Fix \(\zeta>0\), and choose a finite-array interval rule \(\mathcal C_K\) with coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) for every array in \(\mathcal T_K(r)\) and worst expected length at most \(C_{K,\alpha}+\zeta\).  Apply it after the reverse kernel from Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}collision\mbox{-}comparison}\).  For an arbitrary \(\rho\in[-r,r]\), Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}supported\mbox{-}mixture\mbox{-}legality}\) supplies \(q=q_K(\rho)\) with
\[
 |q-\rho|\le\delta_K
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 |L_K-(a-bq)|\le bs_K
\]
on the support of \(\Pi_{K,q}^{\mathrm{shell}}\).  Integrating the finite-array coverage inequality over that supported mixing law shows that, under \(P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\), expanding each endpoint of \(\mathcal C_K\) by \(bs_K\), with clipping to \(\mathcal A\), covers \(a-bq\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).

For later use, couple two marked-Poisson laws at the same intensity by using their common Poisson count and common uniforms for the marks.  The mismatch probability of one mark is
\(c|\rho-q|/2\).  A union bound conditional on the count, followed by expectation, gives
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,\rho},
 P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\right)
 \le\min\{1,\lambda_Kc|\rho-q|/2\}
 \le\min\{1,\lambda_Kc\delta_K/2\}. \tag{14}
\]
Total variation contracts through the reverse kernel.  Thus the triangle inequality, (14), and the reverse comparison show that, under \(P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,\rho}\), expansion of the original interval by \(b(s_K+\delta_K)\) covers \(a-b\rho\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha-u_K\).  Since interval lengths lie in \([0,2br]\), the same comparison and endpoint expansion bound its expected length by
\[
 C_{K,\alpha}+\zeta+2b(s_K+\delta_K)+2br\,u_K. \tag{15}
\]

If any rule has coverage at least \(1-\alpha-u\), independently replace its interval by \(\mathcal A\) with probability
\[
 \gamma(u)=\frac{u}{\alpha+u}.
\]
Its resulting coverage is at least
\[
 \gamma(u)+(1-\gamma(u))(1-\alpha-u)=1-\alpha, \tag{16}
\]
and its expected length increases by at most \(2br\gamma(u)\).  Applying (16) to (15), and then letting \(\zeta\downarrow0\), proves
\[
 C_\alpha(\lambda_K)
 \le C_{K,\alpha}+2b(s_K+\delta_K)+2br\,u_K
       +\frac{2br\,u_K}{\alpha+u_K}. \tag{17}
\]

Conversely, take a marked-Poisson honest rule at intensity \(\lambda_K\) whose worst expected length is at most \(C_\alpha(\lambda_K)+\zeta\), and apply it to the deterministic collision statistic.  The deterministic part of Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}collision\mbox{-}comparison}\) bounds total variation by \(d_K\), uniformly over arrays.  Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}sharp\mbox{-}cot\mbox{-}endpoint}\) gives the exact target identity \(L_K=a-b\rho_K\).  Coverage therefore falls by at most \(d_K\), and expected length increases by at most \(2brd_K\).  The repair (16), now with \(u=d_K\), is independent of the array.  Letting \(\zeta\downarrow0\) yields
\[
 C_{K,\alpha}
 \le C_\alpha(\lambda_K)+2brd_K
       +\frac{2brd_K}{\alpha+d_K}. \tag{18}
\]

The map \(\lambda\mapsto C_\alpha(\lambda)\) is continuous.  Indeed, for \(\lambda,\lambda'\ge0\), couple the smaller-intensity Poisson process to the larger by adding an independent Poisson count of mean \(|\lambda-\lambda'|\), marked with the same parameter \(\rho\).  Uniformly in \(\rho\), the observations agree with probability at least \(e^{-|\lambda-\lambda'|}\).  Hence, with
\[
 v(\lambda,\lambda')=1-e^{-|\lambda-\lambda'|},
\]
any honest rule at either intensity, when used at the other, loses at most \(v(\lambda,\lambda')\) in coverage and at most \(2brv(\lambda,\lambda')\) in expected length.  Applying (16) in both directions gives
\[
 |C_\alpha(\lambda)-C_\alpha(\lambda')|
 \le2brv(\lambda,\lambda')
   +\frac{2brv(\lambda,\lambda')}{\alpha+v(\lambda,\lambda')}, \tag{19}
\]
which tends to zero with \(|\lambda-lambda'|\).

Suppose now that \(\lambda_K\to\lambda<\infty\).  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}vanishing\mbox{-}triples\mbox{-}implies\mbox{-}growing\mbox{-}cells}\) gives \(K\to\infty\).  Since \(\lambda_K\) is bounded, the definition of \(s_K\) gives, for all large \(K\),
\[
 s_K=\{K(1\vee\lambda_K)\}^{-1/4}\to0,
 \qquad
 Ks_K^2=\sqrt{K/(1\vee\lambda_K)}\to\infty.
\]
Consequently \(\eta_K\to0\), \(\delta_K\to0\), and Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}vanishing\mbox{-}triples}\) gives \(e_K,u_K,d_K\to0\).  Combining (17)--(19) proves
\[
 C_{K,\alpha}\longrightarrow C_\alpha(\lambda). \tag{20}
\]

We next verify the finite interval programs in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}certified\mbox{-}interval\mbox{-}lp}\).  This certification claim is on the domain specified by that definition: \(\lambda\), all other fixed real inputs, and all nonrational grid nodes are supplied by computable-real oracles.  The total-variation modulus used there follows from the coupling that proved (14): for all \(\rho,\rho'\in[-r,r]\),
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda,\rho},
 P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda,\rho'}\right)
 \le\omega_\lambda(|\rho-\rho'|)
 :=\min\{1,\lambda c|\rho-\rho'|/2\}. \tag{21}
\]
Thus an event probability changes by at most this quantity, and the expectation of an interval length, which takes values in \([0,2br]\), changes by at most \(2br\omega_\lambda\).

The stated overflow certificate is also valid.  If \(\lambda=0\), then \(\tau_m(0)=0\).  If \(0<\lambda<m+1\), exponential Markov inequality gives, for \(t>0\),
\[
 \Pr\{N\ge m+1\}
 \le\exp\{\lambda(e^t-1)-t(m+1)\}.
\]
The minimizing positive value is \(t=\log((m+1)/\lambda)\), whence
\[
 \tau_m(\lambda)
 \le e^{-\lambda}\left(\frac{e\lambda}{m+1}\right)^{m+1}. \tag{22}
\]

For the lower certificate, start from an arbitrary continuum-honest interval rule.  On each retained state \(x\in\mathsf X_m\), replace its reported interval by the shortest action in \(\mathsf A_h\) spanning precisely the grid targets that it contains; if it contains no grid target, use the null pattern.  This preserves membership of every grid target and does not increase length.  Removing the overflow states loses at most \(\tau_m(\lambda)\) in coverage.  The resulting weights therefore satisfy the exact lower program's coverage and length constraints with an objective no larger than the continuum rule's worst expected length.  Replacing coverage coefficients upward and their right sides downward can only enlarge this feasible set; replacing length coefficients and lengths downward can only decrease its recorded objective.  Taking the infimum over continuum-honest rules proves
\[
 D_{m,h,s}^-\le C_\alpha(\lambda). \tag{23}
\]

For the upper certificate, take an exact rational feasible solution of the directed upper program.  Because every retained coverage coefficient and the overflow probability were rounded downward while \(1-\alpha\) was rounded upward, its actual gridwise coverage is at least \(1-\alpha\).  Because every length contribution was rounded upward, its actual expected length at every grid node is no greater than \(P_{m,h,s}^+\).  Give the overflow state the action \(\mathcal A\).  For arbitrary \(\rho\), choose a nearest grid point \(\rho_j\); the maximum-gap condition gives \(|\rho-\rho_j|\le h/2\).  If an unexpanded action covers \(a-b\rho_j\), its expansion \(E_h\) covers \(a-b\rho\).  By (21), with
\[
 \omega_h=\min\{1,\lambda ch/4\},
\]
the expanded rule has coverage at least \(1-\alpha-\omega_h\) at \(\rho\).  Applying (16) with \(u=\omega_h\) and \(\gamma_h=\omega_h/(\alpha+\omega_h)\) restores coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) over the entire parameter interval.  Expansion adds at most \(bh\), the change from \(\rho_j\) to \(\rho\) adds at most \(2br\omega_h\) to expected length, and repair adds at most \(2br\gamma_h\).  With the directed upper enclosures stipulated in the definition, this proves
\[
 C_\alpha(\lambda)\le
 P_{m,h,s}^++bh+2br\omega_h+2br\gamma_h
 =U_{m,h,s}^+. \tag{24}
\]
Equations (23)--(24) establish the advertised finite rational bracket.

We record why the certificates are exact.  After directed rounding, both programs have finitely many variables and rational coefficients.  The row-sum constraints put all \(w_{x,A}\) in products of simplices, and one may restrict \(t\) to a bounded interval because the full action is feasible for all sufficiently fine upper roundings.  A linear objective on this compact rational polytope has a minimizing face containing a vertex.  Each vertex solves a finite rational linear system, so it is rational, and finite basis enumeration finds the least objective exactly.  For the lower program, exact feasibility of a rational dual vector and equality of its objective with the enumerated primal value certify optimality by the algebraic weak-duality identity.  Equivalently, such multipliers exist because at a minimizing vertex the objective vector belongs to the cone generated by the active constraint normals: otherwise a separating direction would preserve all active inequalities locally and strictly decrease the objective.  This also shows that finite rational primal--dual enumeration terminates.  For fixed \(m,h\), aggregate coefficient error tends to zero with \(s\); when it is less than half the slack \(\alpha\), the rule always reporting \(\mathcal A\) is feasible for the directed upper program.  Thus the stated certificates exist for every fixed \(m,h\) and all sufficiently large \(s\).

Finally we prove contraction of the bracket.  Let \(\xi_s\) denote the sum, in the worst row, of all directed coefficient, right-side, action-length, and correction-term errors.  The aggregate budget in the definition implies
\[
 0\le\xi_s\le C_0 2^{-s}\longrightarrow0, \tag{25}
\]
where \(C_0<\infty\) depends only on the fixed bounded constants, not on the number of states or actions.

First take a continuum-honest rule with worst expected length at most \(C_\alpha(\lambda)+\zeta\).  Replace its action on overflow by \(\mathcal A\), increasing expected length by at most \(2br\tau_m\).  On retained states, round both endpoints outward to adjacent target-grid endpoints.  This preserves coverage, produces an action in \(\mathsf A_h\), and increases length by at most \(2bh\).  Mix this rule with \(\mathcal A\) with probability \(\beta_s=2\xi_s/\alpha\) for all large \(s\) for which \(\beta_s\le1\).  The mixture creates gridwise coverage slack \(\alpha\beta_s=2\xi_s\), enough to absorb both coefficient and right-side rounding errors.  Its directed upper objective is at most
\[
 C_\alpha(\lambda)+\zeta+2br\tau_m+2bh+2br\beta_s+\xi_s. \tag{26}
\]
It is therefore feasible for the rational upper program.  Adding the vanishing expansion, modulus, repair, and correction enclosures in (24) shows
\[
 \limsup U_{m,h,s}^+\le C_\alpha(\lambda) \tag{27}
\]
along every declared refinement, after letting \(\zeta\downarrow0\).

For the opposite side, take an optimal rational lower-program rule.  Interpret its null pattern as a degenerate interval at a point of \(\mathcal A\) that is not a grid target; this has length zero and covers no grid target.  The rounding directions and (25) imply that its actual retained gridwise coverage is at least
\(1-\alpha-\tau_m-\xi_s\), and its actual retained expected length is at most \(D_{m,h,s}^-+\xi_s\).  Report \(\mathcal A\) on overflow, expand each retained interval by \(bh/2\) per endpoint, and transfer from the nearest grid point using (21).  The resulting rule has continuum coverage at least
\[
 1-\alpha-(\xi_s+\omega_h)
\]
and worst expected length at most
\[
 D_{m,h,s}^-+\xi_s+2br\tau_m+bh+2br\omega_h.
\]
One application of (16) with \(u=\xi_s+\omega_h\) makes it honest.  Hence
\[
 C_\alpha(\lambda)
 \le D_{m,h,s}^-+\xi_s+2br\tau_m+bh+2br\omega_h
 +\frac{2br(\xi_s+\omega_h)}{\alpha+\xi_s+\omega_h}. \tag{28}
\]
If \(m\to\infty\), \(h\downarrow0\), and \(s\to\infty\), then (22) and the condition \(m+1>\lambda_s^+\) give \(\tau_m\to0\), while \(\omega_h\to0\) and (25) gives \(\xi_s\to0\).  Equations (23), (27), and (28) imply
\[
 D_{m,h,s}^-\longrightarrow C_\alpha(\lambda),\qquad
 U_{m,h,s}^+\longrightarrow C_\alpha(\lambda),\qquad
 U_{m,h,s}^+-D_{m,h,s}^-\longrightarrow0. \tag{29}
\]

The deterministic-array implementation asserted in the theorem is exactly the construction leading to (18): the transported upper rule loses at most \(d_K\) in coverage and is repaired by one parameter-free mixture with \(\mathcal A\) of probability \(d_K/(\alpha+d_K)\), adding at most \(2brd_K/(\alpha+d_K)\) in expected length.  The supported-mixture reverse construction leading to (17) supplies the matching lower comparison.  Thus both the finite rational certification and the two-sided honest-minimax transfer hold for the actual endpoint \(L_K\), uniformly over the full deterministic-array class.

proposed.statement:
There exist Markov kernels \(\mathsf K_K^{\to}:\mathcal O_K\rightsquigarrow\mathbb N_0^2\) and \(\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow}:\mathbb N_0^2\rightsquigarrow\mathcal O_K\), depending only on \(K,n_0,n_1,a,b,r\) and not on \(q\), such that, with the same parameter \(q\in\mathcal R_K^{\circ}(r)\) indexing both experiments,
\[
 \sup_q\lVert P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\to}-P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le e_K,
 \qquad
 \sup_q\lVert P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow}-P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le e_K,
\]
where \(e_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K\}\). Both sides attach the decision target \(a-bq\) to the index \(q\). Moreover, for every deterministic array in \(\mathcal T_K(r)\), the law of \((M_K,S_1,\ldots,S_{M_K})\) is within \(e_K^{\mathrm{det}}=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\lambda_K^2/(2K)\}\) in total variation of \(\mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho_K}\), uniformly over arrays.
proposed.justification: Two-sided comparison and uniform deterministic approximation are the information-theoretic bridge from the causal endpoint to a tractable non-Gaussian experiment.
proposed.gap: Arratia, Goldstein, and Gordon provide forward Poisson approximation, while Kipnis's Theorems~2.1 and~2.3 provide one-sample supported-mixture conditioning and fixed-count transfer; neither supplies two parameter-free marked two-arm kernels on the finite correlation lattice or uniform approximation centered at every realized array target.
proposed.consumer: Any bounded-loss estimator or interval designed in the marked-Poisson experiment can be transported back to the finite covariate partition with an explicit error budget.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof directly invokes the frozen cited Chen--Stein dependency-neighborhood lemma, so that cited leaf must be recorded in the theorem's dependency spine.

proposed.statement:
If \(\lambda_K\to\lambda\in[0,\infty)\), then \(C_{K,\alpha}\to C_\alpha(\lambda)\). For every computable \(\lambda\), every \(m,h\), and all sufficiently large certification precisions \(s\), the procedure \(\operatorname{LP}_{m,h,s}^{\mathrm{int}}(\lambda)\) returns exactly verified rational values satisfying
\[
 D_{m,h,s}^-\le C_\alpha(\lambda)\le U_{m,h,s}^+.
\]
The upper rule uses the overflow action \(\mathcal A\), endpoint expansion \(E_h\), and full-interval repair probability \(\gamma_h\), and therefore has coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) for every \(\rho\in[-r,r]\), not only at grid points. Along any refinement with \(m\to\infty\), \(h\downarrow0\), \(s\to\infty\), and \(m+1>\lambda_s^+\), \(U_{m,h,s}^+-D_{m,h,s}^-\to0\) and both endpoints converge to \(C_\alpha(\lambda)\). Write \(d_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\lambda_K^2/(2K)\}\). Applying the corrected upper rule through the deterministic collision statistic loses at most \(d_K\) in coverage; mixing once more with \(\mathcal A\) with probability \(d_K/(\alpha+d_K)\) restores coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) uniformly over \(\mathcal T_K(r)\) and adds at most \(2br\,d_K/(\alpha+d_K)\) in expected length. The matching lower certificate transfers through the supported-mixture reverse kernel, so the finite-array worst-case expected length converges to \(C_\alpha(\lambda)\).
proposed.justification: Exact honest interval length is the relevant uncertainty frontier when expected collisions remain finite, and rational primal--dual witnesses make that frontier independently auditable.
